result.summary: Aphrodite, posing as a Phrygian princess, tells Anchises she is mortal and that Hermes brought her to be his wife. Anchises, filled with desire, takes her to bed; afterwards she reveals herself as a goddess, calms his fear, foretells their son Aeneas, and tells the story of Ganymedes.

scenes.title: Aphrodite's false tale
scenes.summary: Aphrodite claims to be the daughter of Otreus, carried off by Hermes to be Anchises' wife, and urges him to arrange the marriage. She then puts desire in his heart.
scenes.stakes: Aphrodite risks exposure of her disguise; Anchises risks being deceived into a union with a goddess.

scenes.title: Anchises takes her to bed
scenes.summary: Anchises vows to lie with her whatever the gods do, leads her to his couch and lies with her, unaware she is a goddess.
scenes.stakes: Anchises unknowingly lies with an immortal goddess.

scenes.title: The goddess revealed
scenes.summary: At evening Aphrodite wakes Anchises, now in her divine form. He is terrified and begs not to be left crippled.
scenes.stakes: Anchises fears a palsied, ruined life for having lain with a goddess.

scenes.title: Promise of Aeneas
scenes.summary: Aphrodite reassures him and foretells a son, Aeneas, who will rule the Trojans.
scenes.stakes: Anchises' fear of harm is answered; the line's future is at stake.

scenes.title: Ganymedes and Tros
scenes.summary: Aphrodite recounts how Zeus took Ganymedes to be cupbearer and consoled his grieving father Tros with horses and the news of his son's immortality.
scenes.stakes: Tros grieves for his lost son until Zeus consoles him.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Hermes, who killed the watchman Argus.
Epithet of Aphrodite, linked to the island Cythera.

Anchises voices the danger of union with a goddess.

analysis.text: The hymn shows even Aphrodite, who makes gods love mortals, subject to desire herself, and explains the divine ancestry of Aeneas.
The Trojan royal line, including the Aeneadae, claimed descent from gods; the hymn glorifies that lineage.

legacy.text: Virgil's Aeneid (1st century BC) builds on Aeneas as son of Venus and Anchises.

fun_facts.text: The hymn's explanation of the name Aeneas from the Greek word for 'grief' is a folk etymology.

language_notes.text: 'Slayer of Argus' is Hermes' epithet, recalling his killing of the hundred-eyed giant Argus, set to guard Io. The 'golden wand' is his herald's staff.
'Rapt' means seized and carried off, from Latin raptus; here it is archaic English for abducted.
'Coombes' are deep, wooded valleys or hollows on hillsides.
'Unproved in love' means without experience of sexual love, i.e. a virgin.
'No ill-liking daughter, but a likely' means she will not be disagreeable but suitable and pleasing as a daughter-in-law.
'Bride-piece' means the gifts given to secure a marriage, like a bride-price or dowry.
Anchises refers to the story Aphrodite told him: that she is a Phrygian princess, daughter of Otreus, brought by Hermes to be his wife.
Going down to the house of Hades means dying; he says he would gladly die once he has shared her bed.
Girdle: a belt or sash worn at the waist; loosing it signals undressing and the loss of maidenhood.
Roof-tree: the main roof beam. Cytherea is a title of Aphrodite, linked to the island of Cythera.
Palsied means paralysed or enfeebled; Anchises fears being left crippled or powerless as punishment for lying with a goddess.
The name Aeneas is explained by a pun on the Greek word ainos, 'awful' or 'terrible', echoing her grief.
Tros is the Trojan king, father of Ganymedes; the whirlwind refers to Zeus's abduction of the boy.

context_notes.text: Aphrodite has disguised herself as a young mortal girl to seduce Anchises, a Trojan herdsman of royal descent, as Zeus has willed.
Phrygia lay east of Troy in Asia Minor. Otreus is a king invented by Aphrodite for her cover story.
Apollo, the far-shooter, was a god of the bow whose arrows brought sudden death and plague.
Dardanus was the ancestor of the Trojan royal line, so Anchises is his descendant.
The aegis was Zeus's awe-inspiring goat-skin shield or cloak, so swearing by Zeus who holds it is a solemn oath.
The Guide and slayer of Argus is Hermes, who killed the hundred-eyed giant Argus and guided souls and travellers.

literary_notes.text: The goddess opens by denying she is a goddess; the audience knows she is Aphrodite, while Anchises does not.
She claims 'unbending necessity' compels her, though her own desire and Zeus's design drive the scene; the plea disguises a seduction.
The narrator briefly reveals the divine manipulation behind Anchises' response, showing his love is induced rather than freely chosen.
Laughter-loving Aphrodite is a stock epithet, ironic here as she shyly looks away, hiding her deception.
The mortal's ignorance contrasts with the reader's knowledge, and the narrator stresses the unequal pairing of mortal and goddess.
Hiding his face with his cloak vividly shows his fear and awe on recognising the goddess.
Ganymedes's story is a mythic example: mortals taken by gods can be honoured, comforting Anchises and mirroring his own fate.
Storm-footed horses compresses the horses' swiftness into a compound epithet in the epic manner.
